claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Hf and applying a controlled aging treatment will generate Hf-rich nanoprecipitates in the alloy.
The Hf-rich nanoprecipitates will be fine and coherent.
The Hf-rich nanoprecipitates will be uniformly dispersed in a BCC matrix.
The nanoprecipitates will stabilize the grain structure at high temperatures.
Dislocation pinning by the precipitates will improve high-temperature yield strength.
The proposed precipitate dispersion will improve high-temperature creep resistance.
The intervention will increase high-temperature yield strength by approximately 15–20% relative to the baseline.
The anticipated benefits will hold at approximately 900–1000°C under static or cyclic mechanical loading.
Adding only 1–2 at.% Hf will cause little to no significant increase in overall alloy density.
The Hf addition and aging treatment will preserve room-temperature mechanical performance.
The original alloy without Hf addition or post-aging has a homogeneous BCC structure.
The baseline alloy lacks a fine precipitate-dispersion strengthening mechanism.
The expected benefits depend on keeping the Hf concentration within 1–2 at.%.
The expected benefits depend on optimizing the aging treatment to produce nanoscale precipitates.
Higher Hf concentrations may produce coarse precipitates.
Improper heat treatment may produce coarse precipitates.
Coarse precipitates may embrittle the alloy.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is the original alloy without post-aging, but the experiment applies the same aging treatment to both the baseline and Hf-modified samples. Thus, the experimental control is aged and does not match the defined unaged baseline.

The intervention is defined as the combination of Hf addition and aging, whereas the experiment holds aging constant and varies only Hf. It therefore tests the incremental effect of Hf in aged material rather than the full combined intervention against the stated baseline.
